records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Juliet Samuel had an excellent and comprehensive piece in the Times yesterday on the recent grid shenanigans; it's entitled 'Why are power grid bosses gaslighting us?'
She said:  As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Well, Juliet - we're a day late, but we can tell you what's happening this morning, thanks to David Turver who tweeted that frequency was going up and down like a yoyo - our words, not his. 
What he said was:  And even more frequency oscillations this morning. Frequency above normal operating limit at 6:05, below from 7:14 to 7:22 and then above again from 7:32 to 7:34.  Curiouser and curiouser
Kathryn Porter has just tweeted this:
It's getting embarrassing now... This morning  @neso_energy
has blown through the intraday interconnector trading limits again and like yesterday the frequency has been above and below the safe operational limits
Margins are perfectly fine so I can only think this is a combination of poor modelling and forecasting and the grid constraints affecting the SE
Yesterday saw record balancing costs of just under £50 million so this isn't just a curiosity, it's chaos that's driving bills higher (balancing costs are part of network costs)
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columnists/article/why-are-power-grid-bosses-gaslighting-us-zk5q7ftfm?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Times%20Politics%20-%20Thursday%20October%2015&utm_term=audience_POLITICS
'The first thing to know is that this is not normal. The people who run Britain’s electricity grid want you to think it is, but it isn’t. I believe the psychological term is gaslighting, but given the impending winter gas shortage, that’s optimistic.
The facts are these. In the past fortnight there have been four, maybe five, highly unusual events in the control room of Britain’s electricity grid: major forecasting errors, formal calls to the market for extra power and demands for “emergency assistance” from our neighbours in Europe.
Senior managers at the publicly owned National Energy System Operator (Neso) want you to believe these incidents are “routine”. Since the last “routine” incident in June, which is now the subject of both a technical and a legal investigation, Neso has signed PR contracts worth £400,000 to convince everyone they are doing splendidly. What they haven’t done is learn any lessons or produce any in-depth analysis of what the hell is going on.
Yet things keep happening. On September 28, Neso’s forecasts showed it was going to run out of power and it had to put out a call for extra, same-day (and expensive) generation. After about 15 hours, it cancelled the notice — its forecasts were wrong. On October 6, it issued another call. Luckily, even though the wind was low, demand was lower. Again, the forecasts were wrong.
On October 9, for no obvious reason, the grid suddenly ran so short of power that its frequency, or “heartbeat”, went out of the normal operating range for ten minutes, which is what happened in June. An internal “frequency event report” on the latest incident, which I’ve seen thanks to a concerned insider, shows that Neso had to push more power from north to south than the wires are meant to take.
It also had to offer a fortune to incentivise power production from generators in the south. When even that wasn’t enough, it issued a call for “emergency assistance” from France. A Neso engineer says we were one circuit trip away from a very serious situation. “All that was left was [to] scramble for emergency assistance from the EU, violate transmission constraints or disconnect demand.”
Incredibly, three days later, Neso was begging France again, issuing its biggest-ever call for power.
Despite plentiful wind on October 12, with cable maintenance slightly overrunning, power couldn’t get down to meet demand in the south. The next day, Tuesday, the grid’s frequency first spiked too high and then fell too low, for reasons as yet unknown. As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Given how often Neso is being caught off guard, I suppose you could argue this is indeed now “routine”. As Andrew Larkins, an energy consultant and former Ofgem adviser, politely puts it: “They’re at risk of normalising something that’s meant to be part of an emergency system … It shows how hard they’re having to work to keep the lights on.” Winter hasn’t even started yet.
Why is this happening? The technical answer is we don’t know because Neso isn’t opening up the incidents to scrutiny in the way that, say, an airliner is forced to facilitate an industry-wide post-mortem when an engine chokes. More successful modernising grids, such as Australia’s, take the opposite approach.
The broader answer is that governments, regulators and owners of the system have indulged a decade of wishful thinking and under-investment, pretending they know how to pull off a radical energy transition when they have devoted appallingly little forethought, planning and money to the question.
The electricity grid used to run off a hundred or so fossil fuel generators, which can be turned up and down on request and are mechanically stable because they spin big, heavy rotors. Demand also tended to follow a pattern. This made balancing power supply and demand fairly straightforward.
Now, large portions of our power (some days, all of it) come from a mix of undersea cables, renewables plants and batteries, all of which can abruptly and unpredictably turn off and on. Small units, such as rooftop solar, don’t even send data to the grid. Customers are using new, variable gadgets like smart meters and electric cars. Forecasting and responding to changes has become, to be technical, a total bloody nightmare. “We can’t see how much reserve we have,” says the engineer.
On top of this, you have a regulator and grid operator moving at the pace of a Siberian town clerk in a Chekhov play. The grid code, which specifies the grid’s technical requirements, is so out of date that when Neso discovered hundreds of wind farms had their meters fitted backwards, so they tell the grid they’re consuming when they’re actually generating, there was no one obvious to blame. But a single technical change to the code can take years of consultations and meetings.
The rules governing grid stability are similarly out of date. A programme to install more granular sensors to monitor frequency in dozens of locations is well overdue. While the US grids have for years had 2,500 such sensors, Britain’s ambition is to have 40 (a tenth of what Larkins says would be equivalent coverage), and even some of those aren’t sharing data in a useable form. A working group on protocols to stop cascades of generator trips, which took out the solar-reliant Iberian grid last year, is crawling along.
It isn’t all Neso’s fault. Private owners of grid infrastructure are in no hurry to make unprofitable improvements. But nor are they being hurried or penalised. Ofgem has repeatedly tolerated grid regulatory failings and delayed or refused investment proposals. As a result, Neso, which ultimately passes costs to users, must now pay a fortune to buy in power on the day it’s needed to avoid blackouts.
Meanwhile, plans to manage the new power system assume we can use advanced software to fine-tune supply and demand. For example, the commercial fridge industry says it can tweak power use up or down. Brilliant! Except that hackers got at supermarket fridges in France this week and cranked them up to 50 degrees. It spoilt a lot of food. If we’re not careful, a hack like that could spoil the grid.
Governments, regulators, operators and owners have all conspired in the delusion that everything is fine and we can keep going at breakneck speed to “clean power 2030”. But the strain is showing and the engineers won’t pretend any more. You can’t run an electricity grid on a news grid.'

A SECOND council has changed how people can object to planning applications after it received an “overwhelming” amount of objections to a proposed AI data centre on the site of a 1000-year-old castle.
Fife Council has confirmed it will no longer accept planning applications by email after it received more than 14,000 representations to plans for a 600MW hyperscale data centre, near Auchtertool, that would see the Hallyards Castle destroyed to make way for the building.
The proposal includes a complex of data hall buildings, which could be as high as 35 metres, around 114 feet, which would be taller than The Kelpies in Falkirk, as well as electricity substations, security fencing, gatehouses and other infrastructure.
It is understood residents were told the change was also in response to the increasing use of AI by respondents.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
There are lies, damned lies and statistics but now there are lies, damned lies and cheap electricity promises.
We have been promised cheap, reliable, green electricity and £300 off our bills for ages but nothing happens.
Figures from Octopus Energy’s “Wasted Wind” tracker shows figures that the wind industry and those of a green disposition would rather be hidden away from sight.
Last year consumers were hit with a bill for £1.47 billion, yes billion, to switch wind farms off and gas plants on. At the end of September this year the figure was £1.5bn. September alone harvested £404 million, with £30m on 30 September. Government analysis, cited in the Octopus Energy report, suggests that annual constraint payments could reach £10bn by 2030. No wonder there is fuel poverty.
One must ask who was the not-so-bright spark who agreed to pay wind turbine owners not to produce electricity. No wonder the cost of UK electricity is among the highest in the world and manufacturing companies cannot compete.
UK households and industry are paying for politicians’ net zero 2050 fixation. Meanwhile most of the rest of the world is harvesting and burning cheap fossil fuels, predominantly coal, to drive their economies.
Clark Cross Linlithgow, West Lothian 
Of the many recent letters praising Scotland’s renewable energy capabilities none have addressed the most essential factor – the efficiency of the total network system.
The simplest metric for this is constraint payments. For the last complete year 96 per cent of UK payments went to Scottish generators, so by some margin we have the least efficient part of the system, and this can only get worse if Torness is replaced by yet more intermittent generation.
A Mccormick Terregles, Dumfries

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
One thing that has frustrated me for years is the glaring inconsistency in how environmental regulation is applied in Australia.
During my forestry career in Tasmania, the protection of wedge-tailed eagles was taken extremely seriously. Forestry operations followed detailed environmental prescriptions designed to avoid disturbing breeding birds, including exclusion zones around active nests and seasonal operating restrictions. Compliance was built into every harvest plan and it wasn't optional.
Now compare that with what is emerging from some wind energy developments. Reports that 20 wedge-tailed eagles have been killed at the Rye Park Wind Farm in just 18 months have renewed calls for stronger wildlife protections and bird-strike mitigation technology.
I find that contrast difficult to ignore. Forestry was heavily regulated because it could disturb threatened species. Wind farms are being approved and operated in landscapes where there is a foreseeable risk of actually killing them.
I want to know why similar environmental values are regulated so differently depending on the industry involved. When forestry sought approval to operate, the burden of proof rested squarely on demonstrating that impacts on threatened species would be avoided or minimised. Failure to meet those requirements meant an operation couldn't proceed.
However, when protected birds are killed by wind turbines, the response often seems to be retrospective — monitor the deaths, trial new technologies, or adjust operations after the fact — rather than asking whether the project was appropriately located in the first place.
If the precautionary principle is genuinely important, it should apply equally to every form of development. Environmental protection should not depend on whether a project is labelled "renewable". The same threatened species deserves the same level of protection whether the risk comes from forestry, mining, urban development or wind energy.
Conservation loses credibility when one industry faces rigorous precautionary regulation while another is largely judged after the damage has already occurred.
ABOUTREGIONAL.COM.AU Wedge-tailed eagle deaths at NSW wind farm spark calls for stronger wildlife protections | About Regional

Glasgow Airport opens solar farm set to supply 25% of its electricity. The 10MW development is expected to save around 1,100 tonnes of CO2 equivalent every year
The 10MW development, on airport land near Barnsford Road, comprises more than 14,300 photovoltaic panels.
It forms part of AGS Airports’ new Horizons sustainability strategy and is expected to save around 1,100 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent each year, based on grid electricity emissions.
The airport operator said it has reaffirmed its commitment to achieving net zero for its own emissions by 2035 and is now proposing similar infrastructure at Aberdeen International and Southampton airports.
The project has been underpinned by its partnership with SP Energy Networks (SPEN), the electricity network operator for central and southern Scotland.— at Glasgow Airport.

records.bodyText:
Greater Providence
NationalPoliticsCrimeWeatherFoodArtsMore
Wreck Believed To Be Rhode Island Boat Found Feet From Wind Turbine, Reviving 2019 Mystery
By Maya Bushman
Published on October 14, 2026
Providence
https://hoodline.com/.../wreck-believed-to-be-rhode.../
More than seven years after the F/V Mistress vanished into frigid New Year's Day seas off Block Island, divers have located wreckage believed to be from the vessel in about 92 feet of water — roughly 50 feet from the base of Turbine No. 1 at the Block Island Wind Farm. Side-scan sonar and underwater photographs documented the site, reigniting scrutiny of a tragedy that claimed two local fishermen and left a lone survivor with a harrowing story of escape.
The 52-foot wooden trawler sank after radioing that it was taking on water in the early hours of January 1, 2019, according to 1420 WBSM. A NOAA incident report filed after the sinking found that the vessel began flooding off Block Island and capsized once its dewatering pumps could no longer keep pace with incoming seawater, as documented by The Scuba News. The boat carried a crew of three; only one man survived.
A Family Boat, A Family Loss
Captain Oscar Diaz and deckhand John Ansay Jr., who was also Diaz's nephew, were lost in the sinking, per the station's report. Tim Diaz was pulled from a life raft and rescued by the crew of the F/V Captain Bligh, according to the same account. The Mistress was owned by Hope Fisheries, Inc. and worked out of Point Judith, Rhode Island, according to Latti Associates LLC.
The scale of the original search underscored how dire conditions were that night. The Coast Guard deployed multiple cutters, an aircraft, and heavy-weather motor lifeboat crews from Station Menemsha, covering 2,152 square nautical miles over 72 hours before suspending active rescue efforts, according to MV Times. The Coast Guard's search continued beyond survivability models for people in winter seas wearing survival suits, per the same outlet.
Helicopter Search Cut Short Near Turbines
Coast Guard search-and-rescue logs from that night show an MH-60T Jayhawk helicopter aborted its search for the Mistress crew after roughly 37 minutes, citing severe weather, poor visibility, and proximity to the wind turbines, according to National Fisherman. The Coast Guard's investigation reached no conclusions about the sinking, and the Coast Guard later conducted training at the Block Island Wind Farm.
Fishing boats searched the area, and offers of help came in.
Divers Document Wreckage And Possible Remains
Scientific divers sponsored by Green Oceans inspected the seabed site in August 2026, documenting features consistent with a wreck believed to be the Mistress, including its propeller, shaft, fuel tanks, net drum, and deck hatch, along with apparent human remains, according to The Scuba News. Green Oceans marine professionals first located the site using side-scan sonar in July 2026, per National Fisherman's reporting. Green Oceans is a nonprofit that opposes offshore wind development off the Massachusetts and Rhode Island coasts, and believes there could be a link between the sinking and the wind farm's presence.
Michael Lombardi, president of Green Oceans, said the wreck's orientation merits investigating whether the crew made an emergency turn to starboard to avoid colliding with a turbine, per Fox News Digital. With the hull already full of water, he said, that kind of maneuver could have caused the vessel to roll and sink. The Coast Guard's original investigation reached no conclusions about the cause of the sinking, and Green Oceans has openly criticized how that inquiry was handled.
Push To Reopen The Investigation
Green Oceans has submitted side-scan sonar imagery and dive photos to the Coast Guard, the National Transportation Safety Board, and Rhode Island authorities, and has asked the Department of the Interior to coordinate an investigation, according to Newport Buzz. The group says the discovery raises broader questions about how rescuers can safely assist distressed vessels near offshore wind turbines in the rough conditions routinely encountered off the Northeast coast.
The Block Island Wind Farm, commissioned in December 2016 as the first commercial offshore wind project in the United States, consists of five 6-megawatt turbines standing 600 feet tall, about 3.8 miles off Block Island, according to background compiled by the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. The facility has a capacity of 30 megawatts. Concerns have been raised about navigation and search-and-rescue near turbines.
For now, federal regulators at the Coast Guard and NTSB have not said whether they will reopen the case, and the identity of the human remains found at the wreck site has not been confirmed. Those questions remain open more than seven years after the Mistress went down, leaving Point Judith's fishing community, and the family of John Ansay Jr., still waiting for answers.
HOODLINE.COM Wreck Believed to Be F/V Mistress Found Near Block Island Wind Turbine

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
We've chosen this image to introduce this post, because it reminded us of what we said yesterday regarding John Campbell's courtesy in his delivery of NOTKUP's closing submission.  He has the same courteous manner in any hearings in which we've watched him over the years, but wallop he certainly did.
And, although comparisons are said to be odious, the same can't be said, in our opinion, for his fellow KC Paul Reid whose combative attitude we've noticed throughout the hearings on the Beauly to Peterhead OHL.  
Today, we've been going through SSEN's closing submission and it became apparent, very quickly, that the same combative persona came through in the written word as in the oral.
However, that's really beside the point, except that we have now heard so much - and seen so much - about SSEN's lack of consultation and lack of caring for those who will be heavily impacted by their proposals, that we believe it's a fine pairing.
The submission is slightly longer than John Campbell's was and we are going to do no more than highlight some of the sections of it, in as brief a form as possible.
Firstly, as with TKUP but arguably more so, the submission relies on what Ofgem has said by way of ASTI.  This was put into perspective by John Campbell:
'Ofgem’s function is to assess economic and technical need from a transmission system perspective. It is not to conduct the planning and environmental assessment that Parliament has assigned to the Scottish Ministers under s. 37. Neither Ofgem sanction nor politically driven ASTI approval can substitute for this inquiry or discharge the Applicant’s burden of demonstrating compliance with the mandatory content of Sch 9, the Development Plan (including NPF4) and other material considerations.'
An example from the B-P SSEN closing submission:
The Proposed Development is also included within the Accelerated Strategic Transmission Infrastructure (ASTI) framework, through which OFGEM has accepted the strategic need for the project and retains oversight of the efficient expenditure required for its delivery. In this respect, the Applicant is not in the same position as, for example, a commercial entity seeking to develop a renewable energy project for profit. 
A little later they educate the Reporters in what is and isn't a reserved matter.
As explained below, need has, the Applicant submits, been conclusively established by the ASTI framework decision. Looking behind that would “relate to” the reservation. Invariably, conditions will have only a consequential connection with the reservation and so no competence issue arises. A condition that had the effect of fundamentally compromising the Applicant’s ability to deliver the Proposed Development in accordance with the timescales set out in the ASTI framework, however, at least arguably relates to (i.e. has more than a loose or consequential connection) with the reservation in para.D1 of sch.5 SA 1998. Accordingly, such a condition would be of doubtful executive competence so far as the Scottish Ministers are concerned.
And
At this stage, the Applicant notices two points. First, rather than ‘salami-slicing’ the Proposed Development is the bringing together of two ASTI projects. Rather than sub-dividing recognised projects, the Application is a consolidation of two projects. Secondly, a detailed cumulative assessment has been done in the EIAR. Any other approach would cause precisely the disproportionate interference with the public interest in the delivery of the ASTI framework (there plainly being a strong public interest in the integrity and reinforcement of the transmission, distribution and supply network) that Sales LJ makes clear the environmental legislation is meant to avoid.
Although the submission goes on to state, in minute detail, most of that which occurred at all the hearings and to round on the people who had given evidence on behalf of the public bodies, particularly The Highland and Moray Councils , the submission disputing what had been said, the submission is light on some things.  Raeshaw, for example, using  EIA regulations to skirt around the subject, in our view.
We've read and heard evidence from so many people about the lack of proper consultation by SSEN and yet there is this:
For completeness, the Applicant notes that a number of complaints were made about the consultation processes which informed the Application. In short, the Applicant maintains that a proper and lawful consultation was undertaken which complied with the common law requirements of such consultations (cf. the “Sedley principles”: R v Brent London Borough Council, ex parte Gunning (1985) approved in R (Mosley) v Haringey London Borough Council [2014] . In any event, the lawfulness of those consultations is a matter which is not within the remit of Reporters (or the Scottish Ministers) and the time to challenge the lawfulness of those consultations has long since passed.
An indication of supreme arrogance, in our view.
On Landscape and Visual - 
It has not been disputed that the scale and nature of the Proposed Development is such that significant landscape and visual impacts are to be expected. Accordingly, the question that needs to be addressed is whether those significant landscape and visual impacts are localised and/or are appropriately mitigated. Put shortly, the Applicant’s position is that any significant landscape and visual effects are both localised and appropriately mitigated for the reasons set out in detail in the written evidence and in the summaries of the oral evidence below. Accordingly, the Proposed Development is in accordance with NPF4, Policy 11e)ii.
And
Whether impacts are localised or not - The assessments of the officers at Moray Council and Aberdeenshire Council who determined that the effects of the Proposed Development are localised are commended. THC’s approach, like that of Ms Anderson and Moray Council (contrary to the professional judgement of its officers), is at odds with the deliberate wording of NPF4 Policy 11e)ii. It would preclude the consent of any strategic OHL in fundamental conflict with NPF4’s overarching spatial strategy to deliver net-zero transmission infrastructure.
A little later, Aberdeenshire officers were commended.  (In Aberdeenshire Council's closing submission, they are maintaining the same line - approval but with conditions.)
On risk to capercaillie:
In short, NatureScot’s assessment is (a) unduly precautionary, (b) inconsistent with its own guidance and its responses to other projects, and (c) not supported by established science. It should not (indeed, cannot) properly be relied upon by the Reporters when formulating their recommendations to Ministers.
There was a slightly gentler tone when referring to closing submissions from non-statutory consultees - the submission referred to:  Dallas Estate; Kirkhill and Bunchrew CC; Fiona Allan, and Save the Deveron Valley.  We also must make mention here of Calum Kemp who had a special section, and see at the end.
The Applicant acknowledges the amount work and time that has been spent, particularly by the local communities, in responding to the Application and participating in the oral processes. Much of their evidence has been addressed in that of the planning authorities and in the further written submissions. Comment here, therefore, is restricted to matters not previously addressed.
Picking out two closing submissions referred to:
Kirkhill & Bunchrew CC - need for the Proposed Development has been conclusively established by the UK Government’s ASTI Framework decision. It is set out in detail in the EIAR and summarised above at paragraphs 13 - 21. In short, the issue that remains is how, not whether, to deliver the Proposed Development (and the other 24 ASTI projects). The Applicant’s position in respect of the decision in Raeshaw Farms Ltd v Scottish Ministers 2026  is set out in the further written submissions dated 14  & 28  May 2026 and 28 August 2026 . As noted above, nothing in Raeshaw questioned or sought to depart from the established authorities. The criticism was specific to that case such that the legal framework in which the evaluation falls to be carried out is unchanged. The Applicant’s positions in respect of the Fanellan substation and traffic and transportation are fully set out it the further written submissions dated 28 May and 11 June 2026.
Fiona Allan - The devolved competence of Scottish Ministers is set out above at Part C. The Applicant relies on its further written submissions and Part C above in respect of the implications of the Raeshaw decision. Similarly, the Applicant relies upon the EIAR and its further written submissions in respect of the effects of the Proposed Development upon ecology, private water supplies, gas pipelines  and public health.
 It is acknowledged that the Proposed Development will result in significant landscape and visual effects. As noted in NPF4 Policy 11e)ii these are to be expected for a project of the scale and nature of the Proposed Development. These effects are localised and/or appropriately mitigated in accordance with NPF4 Policy 11e)ii. As noted in Ms Rylott’s Inquiry Report  route alignment is the first and most effective form of mitigation. Planting and/or landscaping proposals and their subsequent maintenance and management would be secured by condition and management plans.
Calum Kemp's  evidence was more or less dismissed and so was his claim for expenses.
The submission also focused on conditions
..the Chief Planner has recognised that conditions should be framed proportionately, and they should not unduly delay the delivery of nationally important energy infrastructure . The Proposed Development is an example of such infrastructure par excellence. A practical application of that approach in respect of the Proposed Development would be providing for mitigation schemes to be agreed before energisation of the OHL (i.e before it comes into operation) rather than before development commences. That latter approach would be bound to delay delivery of the Proposed Development and would the Applicant submits be unreasonable (in the public law sense).
... as set out above at 14 the Proposed Development is presented within the context of the ASTI framework as established by OFGEM as part of its Pathway to 2030.
